title: The greater emptiness
hookLine: a monk who loves company can't find the peace within

lines: ANANDA AND THE MONKS, MAKING ROBES.
A GROUP CHAT THAT NEVER GOES QUIET.
cards: The Buddha is in his home country, at Kapilavatthu. After his meal he goes to the dwelling of a Sakyan named Kalakhemaka, and stops. Beds and mats are laid out everywhere.
Are many monks living here? he wonders. Nearby, Ananda and a group of monks are busy making robes together. It's useful work.
It's also a crowd, like a group chat that buzzes all day, all of it pleasant, none of it quiet. In the evening, the Buddha goes to find Ananda.

teach.b: A monk doesn't shine, the Buddha tells Ananda, who delights in company and loves being part of a crowd. Someone like that can't reach, whenever they wish, the ease of seclusion and peace. Someone who lives withdrawn can.
He isn't scolding the robe-making; he's talking about where delight lives. Then he describes his own abiding: by not attending to any signs, he enters emptiness within. And he gives the method.
First steady the mind inside, quiet it, bring it to one point.
Then attend to emptiness inside. If the mind doesn't settle there, attend to emptiness outside, or both, or to stillness. Know honestly whether it's working.
When he does meet visitors, monks, nuns, lay followers, kings and ministers, his mind still leans toward seclusion, and he talks with them in a way that sends them off. Then talk itself.
If you must speak, speak of fewness of wishes, contentment, solitude, energy, wisdom; not kings and armies and gossip. And at the end, a line about teachers.
I won't treat you, the Buddha says, the way a potter treats damp, unbaked clay, gently.
I'll speak pressing and pressing again. What's sound will stand.
Space inside isn't loneliness. It's a room in the mind that doesn't depend on who else is in the room. You can carry it into a crowd, but first you build it alone.

how: Some Buddhist monastics and lay meditators set aside periods of solitary retreat, and the discourses discourage idle talk about kings, armies and gossip, a list the discourses call 'animal talk'.

o: a strict rule never to speak to anyone
seclusion: a quiet withdrawn from the crowd
being cut off and lonely, against your will

games.q: the greater emptiness: tap the pairs.
p: beds and mats laid out everywhere
how the Buddha won't treat them

s: the Buddha scolds the monks for making robes
he doesn't fault the work; he speaks about delighting in company.
in MN 122 the Buddha still meets kings and lay followers
his mind leans toward seclusion even while he talks with them.
the discourse says emptiness means avoiding people forever
it builds space inside first, and that space is carried into meetings and talk.

games.q: you're steadying the mind inside and attending to emptiness within, but it won't settle. what does MN 122 suggest?
o: give up and join the group.
try emptiness outside, or both, and know honestly whether it's working.
games.why: the Buddha gives options: emptiness inside, outside, both, or stillness, always knowing clearly how it's going.

practice: Turn off what buzzes, if you can, and notice the pull toward company: checking, replying, wondering who's around. Don't fight it; let the mind steady inside, and rest in the space that's here when nobody's talking to you.

wordCard.voice: Viveka. Seclusion, withdrawal: the Buddha tells Ananda that love of company blocks this peace, and teaches emptiness found within, carried even into crowds.

orig.note: Pali viveka: seclusion, withdrawal. the ease of seclusion is what the lover of company can't reach.

carryVoice: Your line: space inside. It travels with you into any crowd you join. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 122, Mahasuññata Sutta (the greater discourse on emptiness)
